Impact assessment converts these into impact categories such as global warming and acidification, and interpretation draws conclusions and opportunities for improvement.

about.h: The functional unit and the system boundary
about.p: The most important thing in an LCA is to compare on the basis of the same function. For a container, for example, the functional unit is not “one bottle” but “delivering 1 L of beverage,” and for lighting it might be “1000 hours of light output.” The basic system boundary runs from raw material extraction to disposal (cradle to grave), though depending on the purpose it may stop at the factory gate (cradle to gate). If the boundaries of the products being compared do not match, the comparison is unfair and overlooks some of one product's burden.

about.h: Use in chemical processes, and cautions
about.p: In chemical processes, LCA is used to compare design options such as choice of feedstock, solvent recovery, heat recovery and use of by-products in terms of CO₂ emissions and the like. Including not only direct emissions within the process but also indirect emissions from producing electricity, steam and raw materials can change the conclusion. Results are affected by how burdens are divided when one process yields several products (allocation) and by how representative the data are, so assumptions are stated explicitly, and sensitivity analysis checks whether the conclusion changes when conditions change.

faq.q: What is LCA?
faq.a: It is a method that compiles the resources used and emissions released over the whole life of a product or service, from raw material extraction through manufacturing, transport and use to disposal, and evaluates the environmental impact.

faq.q: What is a functional unit?
faq.a: It is the amount of function a product performs, used as the basis for comparison. For containers, for example, using “delivering 1 L of beverage” lets products of different volume and weight be compared fairly.

faq.q: Does an LCA always give a single answer?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Results change with the system boundary, assumptions such as the number of reuses and transport distance, the allocation method and the data used, so the assumptions are stated and checked with sensitivity analysis.

ファラデーの法則.desc: The law that the amount of substance reacting at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed, with a z-electron reaction needing a charge of zF per mole. F is about 96485 C/mol.

about.p: Faraday's laws of electrolysis state that the amount of substance reacting at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed (first law), and that the amount reacting for the same charge is inversely proportional to the number of electrons involved (second law). Together they give the amount produced as n [mol] = Q/(zF) = It/(zF). F is the Faraday constant, the charge of 1 mol of electrons, 96485 C/mol. For example, passing 10 A for 1 hour (3.6×10⁴ C) deposits about 0.187 mol, or about 11.9 g, of copper in its two-electron reaction.

In real electrolysis, part of the charge passed is used for side reactions, back reactions of the product and leakage currents, so the amount produced is less than the theoretical amount from Faraday's law. The ratio is the current efficiency, and the actual amount produced = current efficiency × It/(zF). Conversely, when finding the current from the amount needed, divide by the current efficiency. Current efficiency changes with electrolyte composition, temperature, current density and electrode material, so it is an important measure when setting operating conditions. For example, depositing 11.9 g of copper at 90% current efficiency takes about 1.11 hours at 10 A.

Electrical energy is charge × cell voltage, so the energy per mole of product is zFV/(current efficiency). Converted per tonne of product or per Nm³ of hydrogen, this is the specific energy consumption. Producing 1 Nm³ of hydrogen (about 44.6 mol) at a cell voltage of 2.0 V and 100% current efficiency takes about 4.8 kWh, and producing 1 t of NaOH at 3.0 V and 95% takes about 2100 kWh. Note that z is set by the number of electrons that flow per mole of product.

faq.q: What is the equation of Faraday's law?
faq.a: The amount produced is n = It/(zF), where I is the current [A], t the time [s], z the number of electrons per mole reacted and F = 96485 C/mol. The mass is found by multiplying n by the molar mass.

faq.q: How is the value of the Faraday constant determined?
faq.a: It is the product of the elementary charge 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ C and the Avogadro constant 6.022×10²³ mol⁻¹, the magnitude of the charge of 1 mol of electrons, about 96485 C/mol.

faq.q: Why is less product obtained than calculated?
faq.a: Because part of the charge goes to side reactions such as hydrogen evolution, back reactions or redissolution of the product, and leakage currents. The fraction that is used is expressed as the current efficiency.

電流効率.desc: The fraction of the total charge passed that is used for the desired reaction. It falls below 100% because of side reactions, back reactions of the product and leakage currents.

槽電圧.desc: The voltage across the two electrodes of an electrolytic cell. It is the theoretical decomposition voltage plus the anode and cathode overpotentials and the ohmic loss, and it rises with current density.

about.p: The cell voltage of an electrolytic cell is broken down as V = E + ηa + |ηc| + IR. E is the theoretical decomposition voltage set by the Gibbs energy change of the reaction, ηa and ηc are the anode and cathode overpotentials, and IR is the ohmic loss from the resistance of the electrolyte, separator, electrodes and conductors. In water electrolysis E = 1.23 V at 25 ℃, but with overpotential and ohmic loss added, the actual cell voltage is often around 1.8–2.0 V, and the difference is lost power. The losses from overpotential and ohmic resistance turn into heat, and the part of the cell voltage above the thermoneutral voltage of 1.48 V appears as net heat generation in the cell.

The theoretical decomposition voltage is set by temperature and concentration and does not depend on current. The overpotential increases roughly in proportion to the logarithm of current density, as in the Tafel equation, and the ohmic loss increases in proportion to current density. Raising the current density therefore reduces the electrode area and capital cost needed for the same production, but raises the cell voltage and worsens the specific energy consumption. The current density of industrial electrolysis is set by balancing capital cost against power cost. Higher current density also increases heat generation, so electrolyte temperature control is considered as well.

Overpotential is reduced with electrocatalysts that speed up the reaction, such as electrodes coated with platinum-group metals or their oxides, and nickel alloys. The dimensionally stable anode (DSA) used in chlor-alkali electrolysis is a typical example. Ohmic loss is reduced by zero-gap designs that narrow the electrode gap, operation at concentrations and temperatures with high conductivity, and structures that let evolved bubbles escape to the back of the electrodes. Bubbles do not conduct electricity, so the more bubbles there are between the electrodes, the higher the effective resistance. Because electrode degradation and impurities in the electrolyte raise the overpotential, the change in cell voltage over time also serves as an indicator of equipment condition.

faq.q: What is cell voltage?
faq.a: The voltage across the two electrodes of an electrolytic cell: the sum of the theoretical decomposition voltage, the anode and cathode overpotentials, and the ohmic losses in the electrolyte and separator.

faq.q: What is the problem with a high cell voltage?
faq.a: Electrical energy is charge × cell voltage, so the specific energy consumption increases in proportion to the cell voltage. The part above the thermoneutral voltage becomes heat, so cooling is also needed.

faq.q: How do current efficiency and cell voltage differ?
faq.a: Current efficiency expresses how much of the charge is used for the desired reaction, and cell voltage expresses the energy used per coulomb of charge. Specific energy consumption is proportional to cell voltage and inversely proportional to current efficiency.

理論分解電圧.desc: The minimum voltage needed for electrolysis, set by the Gibbs energy change of the reaction through E = ΔG/(zF). For splitting water it is 1.23 V at 25 ℃.

過電圧.desc: The extra shift in potential beyond the equilibrium potential needed to drive an electrode reaction at a finite rate. It increases with current density and can be reduced with electrocatalysts.

電力原単位.desc: The electrical energy needed to make one unit of product (1 t or 1 Nm³). In electrolysis it is proportional to the cell voltage and inversely proportional to the current efficiency.

イオン交換膜法.desc: A chlor-alkali process in which a cation-exchange membrane separates the anode and cathode compartments. Na⁺ passes selectively through the membrane, giving chlorine at the anode and high-purity sodium hydroxide and hydrogen in the cathode compartment.

限界電流密度.desc: The current density at which the reactant concentration at the electrode surface falls to zero and the reaction rate is set by mass transfer alone. i_L = zFDC/δ, and it increases with stirring.

透過流束.desc: The amount permeating per unit membrane area per unit time, in m³/(m²·s) or L/(m²·h). In the resistance-in-series model it is proportional to the transmembrane pressure and inversely proportional to the sum of the membrane and cake resistances.

膜間差圧.desc: TMP: the pressure difference between the feed and permeate sides of a membrane, the driving force for membrane filtration. In cross-flow operation the permeate pressure is subtracted from the average of the feed inlet and outlet pressures.

濃度分極.desc: A phenomenon in which solute retained by the membrane accumulates near the membrane surface, so that the surface concentration exceeds the bulk. The film model expresses it as Cm/Cb = exp(J/k).

about.p: In membrane filtration, solute is carried to the membrane surface by the permeating water, but because the membrane retains it, it accumulates near the surface. The accumulated solute diffuses back into the bulk down the concentration difference, and at steady state convection toward the membrane balances back-diffusion, forming a layer of high concentration at the surface. This is concentration polarization. When the solute is completely rejected, the film model gives the ratio of surface to bulk concentration as Cm/Cb = exp(J/k), where k = D/δ is the film mass transfer coefficient.

In reverse osmosis, a higher surface concentration raises the osmotic pressure at the surface, so the effective pressure difference shrinks at the same operating pressure and the permeate flux falls. The permeate concentration also rises with the surface concentration, so the observed rejection calculated from the bulk concentration falls. In ultrafiltration, when the surface concentration of macromolecules reaches the gel concentration a gel layer forms, and the flux levels off and no longer increases with pressure. Concentration of salts at the surface is also a cause of scale precipitation. RO design therefore evaluates osmotic pressure and scale precipitation at the membrane-surface concentration.

Concentration polarization strengthens exponentially as J/k increases, so the basic approach is to increase the mass transfer coefficient k. The boundary layer is thinned by raising the cross-flow velocity, inserting spacers (turbulence promoters) in the channels and designing the module shape. Operating without pushing the flux too high also helps. For example, at J/k = 0.5 the surface concentration is about 1.65 times the bulk, and at J/k = 1 about 2.7 times. In stirred test cells, k is determined by varying the stirring speed, and the true rejection is estimated from it.

faq.q: Are concentration polarization and fouling the same thing?
faq.a: No. Concentration polarization is a concentration profile in which solute accumulates near the membrane surface during operation, and it disappears when operation stops. Fouling is the attachment of material to the membrane surface or pores; it remains after stopping and requires cleaning.

faq.q: What is the film model equation?
faq.a: When the solute is completely rejected, Cm/Cb = exp(J/k). When some solute leaks into the permeate, (Cm − Cp)/(Cb − Cp) = exp(J/k).

faq.q: Why does the observed rejection fall?
faq.a: Because the surface concentration becomes higher than the bulk and the permeate concentration rises too. Based on the bulk concentration the rejection comes out lower. The rejection based on the surface concentration is the true rejection.

阻止率.desc: The fraction of solute held back by a membrane, R = 1 − Cp/C. There is the observed rejection based on the bulk concentration and the true rejection based on the membrane-surface concentration.

分画分子量.desc: A value expressing the performance of UF and similar membranes: the molecular weight at which the rejection of standard substances reaches a set value (often 90%). Also written MWCO.

ファウリング.desc: A loss of permeability caused by deposition on the membrane surface or by adsorption and blockage inside the pores. Some is reversible by backwashing, and some requires chemical cleaning.

about.p: Fouling is the loss of membrane permeability as operation continues. By cause it is divided into deposition of suspended solids (cake layers), adsorption of organics such as proteins and humic substances, inorganic scale such as calcium carbonate and silica, and biofouling, in which microorganisms grow on the membrane surface. By location, there is fouling that builds up on the membrane surface and fouling that blocks the inside of the pores; it shows up as a rise in transmembrane pressure in constant-flux operation and as a fall in permeate flux in constant-pressure operation. Because lower water temperature raises viscosity and lowers flux, temperature correction is essential to distinguish this from fouling.

Fouling that is recovered by physical cleaning such as backwashing, air scouring or flushing is called physically reversible, and fouling that is not is called irreversible. Cake layers on the surface are often reversible, while adsorption inside the pores and firmly attached scale tend to be irreversible. The irreversible part is treated by chemical cleaning, using sodium hypochlorite or alkali for organics and acids such as citric acid or hydrochloric acid for inorganic scale, and what still does not recover determines the membrane's life. The timing of cleaning is decided, for example, when the transmembrane pressure reaches a preset upper limit.

Pretreatment such as coagulation and filtration reduces suspended solids, and in RO, adding antiscalants and limiting the recovery prevent scale from precipitating. In MF and UF, periodic backwashing, operation at fluxes below the critical flux, and shear at the membrane surface from cross-flow or aeration are effective. In terms of the resistance-in-series model J = TMP/{μ(Rm + Rf)}, the flux halves as soon as the fouling resistance Rf becomes comparable to the membrane resistance, so early action is important. When handling liquids that foul easily, as in MBRs, the membrane surface is scoured continuously by aeration.

faq.q: How can fouling be detected?
faq.a: It shows up as a rise in transmembrane pressure in constant-flux operation and as a fall in permeate flux in constant-pressure operation. Comparisons are made after correcting for viscosity changes with water temperature.

faq.q: What is backwashing?
faq.a: A physical cleaning in which permeate is passed through the membrane in the reverse direction to push out the cake layer and blockages at the pore entrances. It is done at fixed intervals for MF and UF membranes.

faq.q: What chemicals are used for chemical cleaning?
faq.a: Sodium hypochlorite or sodium hydroxide for organics and microorganisms, and acids such as hydrochloric acid or citric acid for inorganic scale, within the limits of the membrane's chemical resistance.

分離係数.desc: A value expressing how readily two components are separated by a membrane. For gas separation membranes it is the permeability ratio PA/PB, and in pervaporation the ratio of the composition ratios of permeate and feed.

浸透気化.desc: Membrane separation in which the permeate side is kept under vacuum so that components passing through the membrane from a liquid feed are withdrawn as vapor. It is used, for example, to dehydrate azeotropic mixtures.

理論空気量.desc: The minimum amount of air needed to burn a fuel completely. It is obtained by finding the theoretical oxygen from the fuel composition and dividing by the O₂ fraction of air (21 vol%).

空気比.desc: The ratio m of the air actually supplied to the theoretical air. The excess air, as a fraction of the theoretical air, is m − 1. Gaseous fuels are fired at smaller values and solid fuels at larger ones.

about.p: The air ratio m is the air actually supplied, A, divided by the theoretical air A₀: m = A/A₀. With exactly the theoretical air m = 1, and the fraction supplied beyond that is the percent excess air, m − 1. Some fields use the fuel-to-air ratio instead, and the equivalence ratio φ, the fuel-to-air ratio divided by its stoichiometric value, equals 1/m. φ < 1 (m > 1) is called lean and φ > 1 (m < 1) rich. In combustion calculations, the theoretical oxygen and theoretical air are found from the fuel composition, and the actual air is then set by multiplying by the air ratio. In English texts the same quantity is often written λ (the air–fuel equivalence ratio) and is sometimes called the excess air ratio; do not confuse it with the excess air m − 1. In English texts the same quantity is often written λ (the air–fuel equivalence ratio) and is sometimes called the excess air ratio; do not confuse it with the excess air m − 1.

about.h: Effect on flue gas and efficiency
about.p: Raising the air ratio does not increase the heat released by the fuel, but the extra air leaves as flue gas, so the flue gas volume and the flue gas loss increase and the flame temperature falls. If the air ratio is below 1, oxygen is insufficient and CO, soot and unburned hydrocarbons remain, so not all of the fuel's heat is recovered. Because real equipment mixes imperfectly, the air ratio is kept as small as possible without producing unburned matter. Typical values are about 1.05–1.2 for gaseous fuels, somewhat larger for liquid fuels and about 1.2–1.5 or more for solid fuels, though they vary with the equipment.

about.h: Finding the air ratio from flue gas analysis
about.p: With complete combustion, the O₂ in the flue gas is only what was contained in the excess air. If the dry flue gas volume is taken as roughly equal to the air supplied, the O₂ concentration [%] is 21(m − 1)/m, and the air ratio can be estimated as m = 21/(21 − O₂). At 5% O₂ this gives about 1.31, and at 3% about 1.17. Once the fuel is fixed, the CO₂ concentration in the dry flue gas for combustion with theoretical air (CO₂max) is also fixed, so m ≈ CO₂max/CO₂ can be used as well. In boilers and furnaces, combustion control that adjusts the air flow by continuously measuring flue gas O₂ is widely used.

faq.q: What is the difference between the air ratio and percent excess air?
faq.a: The air ratio m is the ratio of actual air to theoretical air, and the percent excess air is the fraction of extra air supplied, m − 1. An air ratio of 1.2 corresponds to 20% excess air.

faq.q: Is a larger air ratio always safer and more efficient?
faq.a: It reduces unburned matter, but the extra air is heated and discharged, so the flue gas loss rises and the efficiency falls. The basic rule is to keep it as small as possible without producing unburned matter.

faq.q: How is it related to the equivalence ratio?
faq.a: The equivalence ratio φ is the fuel-to-air ratio divided by its stoichiometric value, which is the reciprocal of the air ratio: φ = 1/m. It is used mainly for premixed combustion and engines.

発熱量.desc: The heat released when a unit quantity of fuel burns completely. There is the higher heating value, which counts the water formed as liquid, and the lower heating value, which counts it as vapor.

about.p: The heating value is the heat released when 1 kg or 1 Nm³ of fuel burns completely and the combustion products are cooled back to the initial temperature (usually 25 ℃). The value counted with the water formed condensed to liquid is the higher heating value (gross heating value, HHV), and the value counted with it left as vapor is the lower heating value (net heating value, LHV); the difference is the latent heat of vaporization of the water formed and of the moisture in the fuel. For methane the HHV is about 890 kJ/mol and the LHV about 802 kJ/mol, and the difference of about 88 kJ corresponds to the latent heat of 2 mol of water. The heating value is a property of the fuel and does not change with the air ratio or air preheating.

For liquid and solid fuels, 1 kg of hydrogen forms 9 kg of water, so the conversion is LHV = HHV − latent heat × (9h + w), where h is the mass of hydrogen and w the mass of moisture per kg of fuel, and the latent heat is about 2.44 MJ/kg at 25 ℃. For example, a fuel with an HHV of 46.0 MJ/kg and 14% hydrogen forms 1.26 kg of water, giving an LHV of about 42.9 MJ/kg. The more hydrogen a fuel contains, the larger the difference: about 10% for natural gas, about 6% for heavy fuel oil and about 15% for hydrogen itself.

In ordinary boilers and furnaces that do not condense the water vapor in the flue gas, the heat that can be recovered is at most the LHV, so efficiency is often stated on an LHV basis, as for much equipment in Europe and Japan. In North America and elsewhere the HHV basis is also widely used, and the efficiency figure of the same equipment differs by a few percent to about 10% depending on the basis. In condensing boilers, which cool the flue gas below its dew point to recover the latent heat as well, the LHV-based efficiency is sometimes shown as above 100%. When comparing efficiencies, always check which basis is used.

faq.q: Which is larger, the HHV or the LHV?
faq.a: The higher heating value (HHV), which includes the latent heat of condensation of the water formed, is larger. The difference is the latent heat of vaporization of the water formed and of the moisture in the fuel.

faq.q: How is the lower heating value calculated?
faq.a: For liquid and solid fuels, LHV = HHV − 2.44 × (9h + w) [MJ/kg] is a good guide, where h is the mass of hydrogen and w the mass of moisture [kg] per kg of fuel.

faq.q: Why can an efficiency exceed 100%?
faq.a: Because the efficiency of equipment that condenses the water vapor in the flue gas and recovers its latent heat is expressed relative to the LHV, which excludes that latent heat. On an HHV basis it does not exceed 100%.

排ガス損失.desc: The heat carried away by flue gas leaving at a temperature above the reference temperature. It is roughly proportional to the flue gas volume and temperature and is reduced by proper air ratios and waste heat recovery.

予混合燃焼.desc: Combustion in which fuel and air are mixed before burning. It burns fast and allows high loads, but flashback occurs when the flow velocity falls below the burning velocity.

ウォッベ指数.desc: The heating value of a gaseous fuel divided by the square root of its specific gravity. With the same nozzle and supply pressure the heat input is proportional to it, so it is used to judge gas interchangeability.

サーマルNOx.desc: Nitrogen oxides formed when N₂ in the combustion air is oxidized at high temperature. They increase sharply with flame temperature and are suppressed by flue gas recirculation and staged combustion.

酸露点.desc: The temperature at which sulfuric acid vapor formed from SO₃ and water vapor begins to condense. It is far above the water dew point, and heat transfer surfaces below it suffer low-temperature corrosion.

成績係数.desc: The COP, a measure of the efficiency of refrigerators and heat pumps: the heat absorbed (cooling) or rejected (heating) divided by the power input. The heating value is 1 larger than the cooling value.

about.p: The coefficient of performance (COP) is the ratio of the useful heat obtained to the power input W. A refrigerator uses the heat QL removed from the cold side, so COP = QL/W; a heat pump used for heating uses the heat QH delivered to the hot side, so COP = QH/W. From the energy balance QH = QL + W, the heating COP of a given cycle is always exactly 1 larger than its cooling COP. Because heat is pumped rather than generated, the value can be well above 1, unlike an efficiency, and household air conditioners show values of about 3–6 under rated conditions.

about.h: Upper limit from the reverse Carnot cycle
about.p: The COP of a refrigerator working between a cold side TL and a hot side TH cannot exceed TL/(TH − TL) of the reversible reverse Carnot cycle, and for a heat pump the limit is TH/(TH − TL). Temperatures must always be absolute. For example, between 5 ℃ and 35 ℃ the limits are about 9.3 for cooling and about 10.3 for heating. The smaller the temperature difference, the higher the limit, so not lowering the evaporating temperature or raising the condensing temperature more than necessary is the basic way to keep the COP high in real equipment as well. Because of irreversible compression and the temperature differences needed for heat transfer, the COP of real machines is often only about half of this limit.

about.h: Points to watch in practical evaluation
about.p: The COP changes greatly with operating conditions. In heat pump heating, the lower the outdoor temperature, the wider the temperature difference and the lower the COP, and defrosting adds to this. Equipment is therefore evaluated not only by a single rated value but also by seasonal averages such as the annual performance factor (APF). When comparing electrically driven equipment with fuel-fired equipment, the comparison must be made in primary energy, including the efficiency of power generation; for example, a heat pump with a COP of 4.0 obtains about 1.8 times as much heat from the same fuel as a 90%-efficient boiler if power generation is 40% efficient.

faq.q: Doesn't a COP above 1 violate conservation of energy?
faq.a: No. A heat pump does not make heat from power; it moves heat from the cold side to the hot side, so the heat moved can exceed the power input.

faq.q: How are the cooling and heating COPs related?
faq.a: For the same cycle, heating COP = cooling COP + 1, because the heat rejected in the condenser is the heat absorbed in the evaporator plus the compressor power.

faq.q: Can Celsius temperatures be used in the Carnot expression?
faq.a: No. The numerator of TL/(TH − TL) must be an absolute temperature; calculating in Celsius gives wrong values such as 0.17 between 5 ℃ and 35 ℃.

蒸気圧縮式冷凍サイクル.desc: A refrigeration cycle that circulates refrigerant through a compressor, condenser, expansion valve and evaporator and absorbs heat by evaporation in the evaporator. Its performance is read from a p-h diagram.

about.h: The four components and refrigerant states
about.p: In the vapor-compression refrigeration cycle, low-pressure refrigerant liquid evaporates in the evaporator by taking heat from the object being cooled, and the vapor is raised to high temperature and pressure by the compressor. The high-pressure vapor rejects heat to cooling water or outdoor air in the condenser and returns to liquid, is throttled in the expansion valve into a low-pressure vapor–liquid mixture, and enters the evaporator again. Used for cooling, the machine is a refrigerator or air conditioner; using the condenser heat for space or water heating makes it a heat pump, and a four-way valve that reverses the refrigerant flow lets one unit do both. The refrigerating capacity is the product of the refrigerant flow rate and the refrigerating effect (the rise in specific enthalpy in the evaporator).

The calculation is simple when the cycle is drawn on a p-h (Mollier) diagram, with pressure (logarithmic) on the vertical axis and specific enthalpy on the horizontal axis. Evaporation and condensation are nearly horizontal lines, compression is a line rising to the right along an isentrope, and the expansion valve is a vertical line of constant enthalpy. Refrigerating effect = h1 − h4, compression work = h2 − h1 and condenser heat rejection = h2 − h3, with h4 = h3 across the expansion valve. For example, with h1 = 400, h2 = 430 and h3 = 250 kJ/kg, the refrigerating effect is 150 kJ/kg, the work 30 kJ/kg and the cooling COP 5.0.

Real refrigerators keep a few kelvin of superheat at the evaporator outlet to prevent liquid from returning to the compressor, and subcool the refrigerant liquid at the condenser outlet to increase the refrigerating effect. For low-temperature duty with large pressure ratios, two-stage compression with intercooling keeps the discharge temperature and power down. Varying the compressor speed with an inverter to raise part-load efficiency is also common. Refrigerants are required to have zero ozone depletion potential and a small global warming potential; besides HFCs, natural refrigerants such as CO₂, ammonia and hydrocarbons and low-GWP HFOs are used.

faq.q: Why isn't a turbine used instead of the expansion valve?
faq.a: Because the power that could be recovered is small compared with the compression power, and an expander handling a liquid-rich flow is complex and expensive. Ordinary refrigerators use simple throttling.

faq.q: What determines the refrigerating capacity?
faq.a: The refrigerant flow rate [kg/s] multiplied by the refrigerating effect h1 − h4 [kJ/kg]. The flow rate is set by the compressor displacement and the specific volume of the suction vapor.

faq.q: How can an air conditioner both cool and heat?
faq.a: A four-way valve reverses the refrigerant flow, swapping the roles of the indoor and outdoor units as evaporator and condenser.

膨張弁.desc: A valve that throttles high-pressure refrigerant liquid down to the evaporating pressure. The change is isenthalpic, and part of the liquid flashes so the temperature falls. Thermostatic types adjust the flow by the superheat.

過熱度.desc: The amount by which a vapor's temperature exceeds the saturation temperature at its pressure. A few kelvin of superheat at the evaporator outlet prevent liquid from returning to the compressor.

吸収式冷凍機.desc: A refrigerator that replaces the compressor by absorbing refrigerant vapor into a solution and regenerating it by heating. There are LiBr–water (water as refrigerant) and ammonia–water systems.

地球温暖化係数.desc: GWP: the warming effect of a gas over a set period (usually 100 years), expressed relative to the same mass of CO₂, taken as 1. It is an important criterion in choosing refrigerants.

湿り空気線図.desc: A chart showing on one sheet the relations among dry-bulb temperature, absolute humidity, relative humidity, specific enthalpy, wet-bulb temperature and more for moist air. It is used to follow changes of state in air conditioning.

顕熱比.desc: SHF: the fraction of an air-conditioning cooling load (total heat) that is sensible heat, which changes temperature. The smaller it is, the more latent heat of dehumidification and the lower the coil temperature needed.

沸点上昇.desc: The rise in the boiling point of a solution containing a nonvolatile solute above that of the pure solvent at the same pressure. In an evaporator it reduces the effective temperature difference to the live steam by the same amount.

about.h: Why it occurs and how large it is
about.p: Dissolving a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapor pressure of the solvent, so a higher temperature than for the pure solvent is needed to boil at the same pressure. In dilute solutions the boiling-point elevation ΔTb is proportional to the molality m of the solute, ΔTb = Kb·m. The molal boiling-point elevation constant Kb of water is about 0.51 K·kg/mol, and for electrolytes the effect is multiplied by the number of ions formed. In the concentrated solutions handled in evaporators this proportionality no longer holds, and some, such as concentrated sodium hydroxide solutions, reach several tens of K, so measured values or Dühring charts are used.

The driving force for heat transfer is the difference between the condensing temperature of the heating steam and the boiling point of the solution. Boiling-point elevation makes the solution boil above the saturation temperature of water at the same pressure, so the effective temperature difference is reduced by the same amount. For example, with heating steam at 120 ℃, a water saturation temperature of 60 ℃ in the vapor space and an elevation of 8 K, the effective temperature difference is 52 K, not 60 K. Designing with the apparent temperature difference leaves the heat transfer area short. Deep in the liquid, the hydrostatic head raises the boiling point further, so this effect is also considered for tall bodies.

about.h: Relation to multiple effects and MVR
about.p: The generated vapor leaves at the boiling point of the solution, but because it is pure solvent vapor it condenses at the saturation temperature of water at the evaporator pressure. The vapor is therefore superheated by the boiling-point elevation, and this superheat is of little use for heating the next effect. In a multiple-effect evaporator the elevation of every effect is subtracted from the overall temperature difference, so the larger the elevation, the harder it is to add effects. In MVR too, the elevation adds to the temperature rise the compression must provide, increasing the compression ratio and power.

faq.q: Does boiling-point elevation depend on the kind of solute?
faq.a: In dilute solutions it does not; it depends on the concentration of dissolved particles (molecules or ions). In the concentrated solutions handled in evaporators, however, differences between solutes are large, and measured values are relied on.

faq.q: Is the generated vapor at the solution boiling point or at the water saturation temperature?
faq.a: The vapor leaves at the boiling point of the solution, but it condenses at the saturation temperature of water. For heat use, think in terms of the water saturation temperature, which is the condensing temperature.

faq.q: How is the effective temperature difference found?
faq.a: Subtract the boiling point of the solution (water saturation temperature + boiling-point elevation) from the condensing temperature of the heating steam. With steam at 120 ℃, a saturation temperature of 60 ℃ and an elevation of 8 K, it is 52 K.

デューリングの法則.desc: The empirical rule that the boiling point of a solution of given concentration is nearly linear in the boiling point of water at the same pressure. Two measurements allow the boiling point at other pressures to be estimated.

蒸気経済.desc: The amount of solvent evaporated per kg of live steam in an evaporator. It is usually a little below 1 for a single effect and increases roughly in proportion to the number of effects in a multiple-effect evaporator.

多重効用蒸発.desc: An arrangement in which the vapor generated in one evaporator body heats the next body at lower pressure. It raises the steam economy, but the bodies share the overall temperature difference, so the heat transfer area increases.

about.h: How it works and the steam economy
about.p: In multiple-effect evaporation, the vapor generated by live steam in the first effect heats the second effect, whose pressure and boiling point are lower, and its vapor in turn heats the third effect, so the same latent heat is used several times. Only the vapor from the last effect is discarded in the condenser, so the steam economy, the evaporation per kg of live steam, rises roughly in proportion to the number of effects N. In practice it is somewhat less than N because of boiling-point elevation, the sensible heat of the feed and heat losses, and it is often estimated at about 0.8 to 0.9 times N, though this varies with conditions.

about.h: Temperature distribution and heat transfer area
about.p: The overall temperature difference, set by the live steam temperature and the condensing temperature of the last effect, minus the boiling-point elevation of each effect, is distributed among the N effects. If each effect is taken to transfer the same heat with the same area, the temperature difference of each effect is inversely proportional to its overall heat transfer coefficient. The temperature difference of each effect is roughly 1/N of that of a single effect, so the total evaporating capacity is not much different from a single effect, and about N times the heat transfer area is needed for the same capacity. Multiple-effect evaporation trades higher equipment cost for lower steam cost.

about.h: Feed arrangements and choosing the number of effects
about.p: Forward feed, which sends the feed from the first effect onward, needs no pumps because the liquid flows by pressure difference, and it finishes the product in the coolest body, which suits heat-sensitive liquids. Backward feed, in which the feed enters the last effect and product is taken from the first, handles the concentrated, viscous liquid at high temperature, which suits solutions whose viscosity rises and cold feeds, but pumps are needed between effects. The number of effects is chosen to minimize the sum of steam and equipment costs, and it is smaller for solutions with a large boiling-point elevation, where the usable temperature difference runs short.

faq.q: Does adding effects increase throughput?
faq.a: Hardly. The effects share the overall temperature difference, so each effect's temperature difference becomes smaller; what mainly increases is the steam economy. To increase throughput, increase the heat transfer area.

faq.q: Why is the last effect operated under vacuum?
faq.a: To lower the boiling point of the last effect and widen the overall temperature difference. The cooling water temperature of the condenser sets the lower limit, and a vacuum pump or ejector removes noncondensable gas to hold the pressure.

faq.q: How do you choose between MVR and multiple effects?
faq.a: MVR is often chosen where electricity is cheap and the boiling-point elevation is small, while multiple effects or thermal vapor recompression are often chosen where steam is cheap or the elevation is large; the two are sometimes combined.

機械的蒸気再圧縮.desc: MVR. A method in which the generated vapor is raised in pressure by a compressor to raise its condensing temperature and returned to heat the same evaporator. It saves a great deal of energy for solutions with a small boiling-point elevation.

熱再圧縮.desc: TVR. A method in which a steam ejector driven by high-pressure live steam draws in part of the generated vapor and the mixed vapor is used for heating. It has no moving parts and is inexpensive.

流下膜式蒸発缶.desc: An evaporator in which the liquid flows down the inner wall of the heating tubes as a thin film and evaporates. The residence time is short and the effect of hydrostatic head is small, so it suits heat-sensitive liquids.

自由度.desc: The number of process variables minus the number of independent equations. Zero means a unique solution, a positive number leaves variables to be fixed by added specifications or optimization, and a negative number means overspecification.

about.p: The degrees of freedom are the number of variables in the problem minus the number of independent equations. The equations include component material balances, energy balances, relations such as vapor-liquid equilibrium, the condition that compositions sum to 1, and conditions from the nature of the unit (for a splitter, equal outlet compositions). It is important not to count dependent equations twice, for example counting the component balances together with the total balance. For a three-component splitter, for example, there are 9 component flow variables and 5 independent equations, giving 4 degrees of freedom.

With zero degrees of freedom, the variables and independent equations balance and the solution is unique (except where nonlinear equations have several solutions). With a positive number, as many flow rates, temperatures, pressures and so on as the degrees of freedom must be given as design specifications, and variables left unspecified can be set by optimization so that an objective function such as cost is best. With a negative number the problem is overspecified with too many equations: the same information is given twice or incompatible conditions are imposed. Counting the degrees of freedom at the start of a design prevents too few or too many specifications.

about.h: Use for units and whole processes
about.p: Adding the degrees of freedom of each unit and subtracting what overlaps in the streams connecting them gives the degrees of freedom of the whole process. For an equilibrium flash of C components, 2 degrees of freedom remain once the feed is fixed: pressure and zero heat duty for an adiabatic flash, or temperature and pressure for an isothermal flash. For a heat exchanger with both inlet conditions and the overall heat transfer coefficient fixed, there is 1 degree of freedom, and either one outlet temperature or the heat transfer area is specified. The warnings in process simulators about missing or excess inputs are based on this counting as well.

faq.q: Is it the same as the degrees of freedom of the phase rule?
faq.a: The ideas are similar but different. Gibbs's phase rule F = C − P + 2 gives the degrees of freedom in intensive variables of a system at equilibrium, while process degrees of freedom are counted over the design variables, including flow rates.

faq.q: What should be done when the degrees of freedom are negative?
faq.a: Check whether the specifications include quantities derivable from the balances or mutually contradictory conditions, and remove the excess ones. When there are redundant measurements, the contradictions may be smoothed out by data reconciliation.

faq.q: How does it relate to optimization?
faq.a: Optimization is choosing the variables left unspecified in a problem with positive degrees of freedom so that the objective function is best. A problem with zero degrees of freedom leaves nothing to choose.

切断流.desc: A stream whose values are guessed to break a loop when a process with recycle is calculated unit by unit. The calculation is repeated until the calculated values agree with the guess.

逐次代入法.desc: A convergence method that repeats the calculation using each result as the next guess. It is simple, but converges slowly in recycle systems with a low single-pass conversion.

感度解析.desc: Analysis of how much the results change when assumed values such as physical properties, prices or rate constants are varied. Comparisons are often made with the relative sensitivity (Δy/y)/(Δx/x).

線形計画法.desc: A method of maximizing or minimizing a linear objective function subject to linear constraints. The optimum appears at a vertex of the feasible region and is found by methods such as the simplex method.

双対価格.desc: The increase in the optimal value of the objective function when the right-hand side of a constraint is relaxed by one unit. It is zero for a constraint that is not used up to its limit.

ピンチ解析.desc: A method that uses composite curves of hot and cold streams or the problem table to find the pinch, which limits heat recovery, and the minimum heating and cooling. It is used to design heat exchanger networks.

about.p: In pinch analysis, the hot streams to be cooled and the cold streams to be heated are represented by composite curves on a temperature-heat diagram. With the hot composite curve always kept above the cold one, the two are brought together until the temperature difference between them is the minimum approach temperature ΔTmin, and the point of closest approach is the pinch. The overlapping range is the heat that can be recovered within the process; the shortfall at the top of the cold side is the minimum heating, and the surplus at the bottom of the hot side is the minimum cooling. The problem table method is used to find them numerically.

In the problem table method, temperature intervals are formed from shifted temperatures, with hot stream temperatures lowered by ΔTmin/2 and cold stream temperatures raised by ΔTmin/2, and in each interval the difference between the sums of the heat capacity flow rates of the hot and cold streams is multiplied by the interval width to give the heat surplus or deficit. The surplus heat is cascaded down from the top interval; the amount needed to cancel the most negative value is the minimum heating, and the temperature where the heat flow becomes zero is the pinch. The heat left at the bottom is the minimum cooling. The overall heat balance alone misses the shortfall caused by temperature constraints.

about.h: Basic design rules and choosing ΔTmin
about.p: To achieve minimum utilities, three rules are followed: do not transfer heat across the pinch, do not cool above the pinch, and do not heat below it. Breaking them increases both heating and cooling by the amount involved. A larger ΔTmin reduces heat recovery and increases utilities, but the larger temperature differences reduce heat transfer area, so the value that minimizes the sum of energy and equipment costs is chosen. There are also placement principles: a heat pump is effective across the pinch, and a heat engine is effective on one side, above or below it.

faq.q: Are the pinch temperatures different for the hot and cold sides?
faq.a: Yes. Relative to the pinch in shifted temperature, it is ΔTmin/2 higher for the hot streams and ΔTmin/2 lower for the cold streams. With a shifted pinch of 115 ℃ and ΔTmin of 10 K, it is 120 ℃ on the hot side and 110 ℃ on the cold side.

faq.q: What determines the difference between minimum heating and minimum cooling?
faq.a: The overall heat balance: it equals the total heat absorbed by the cold streams minus the total heat released by the hot streams. Changing ΔTmin does not change this difference.

faq.q: Can there be no pinch?
faq.a: Yes. In a threshold problem, where only heating or only cooling is needed, the utility is of one kind only over a range of ΔTmin, and its amount may not change as ΔTmin is varied.

最小接近温度差.desc: ΔTmin. The smallest temperature difference kept between hot and cold streams in a heat exchanger network. The larger it is, the more utilities are needed and the less heat transfer area.

準安定域.desc: The region of supersaturation between the solubility curve and the supersolubility curve, where spontaneous nucleation begins. Within it, primary nucleation hardly occurs and seed crystals mainly grow.

about.p: When a solution is cooled, crystals do not appear as soon as it passes the solubility curve and becomes supersaturated. On further cooling, nuclei suddenly form at some temperature, and the line joining these points is the supersolubility curve. The region between the two curves is the metastable zone: new nuclei hardly form there, and growth of existing crystals mainly proceeds. Beyond the supersolubility curve, in the labile zone, primary nucleation occurs explosively and large numbers of fine crystals form. The width of the metastable zone is expressed as the subcooling or supersaturation measured from the solubility curve.

The limit of the metastable zone is not an equilibrium line but a kinetic boundary that includes the waiting time for nuclei to form and grow to a detectable size. It is therefore measured wider at faster cooling rates, and its value also depends on the solution volume and the detection method. Impurities can widen it by hindering nucleation or narrow it by acting as foreign surfaces that promote nucleation. Strong agitation and the presence of crystals promote secondary nucleation, lowering the supersaturation at which nuclei actually start to appear. Unlike the solubility curve, it is not a property intrinsic to the substance, so it should be measured under the conditions of use.

To obtain large, uniform crystals, the supersaturation is kept within the metastable zone, suppressing nucleation and favoring growth. In batch cooling crystallization, seed crystals are added once the solution has crossed the solubility curve into the metastable zone, and cooling is slow at first and faster as the crystal surface area increases. When supersaturation is created by adding antisolvent or by evaporation, the addition rate or heating rate is adjusted so the metastable limit is not exceeded locally. Conversely, when fine particles are wanted, the solution is driven quickly into the labile zone at high supersaturation to generate many nuclei.

faq.q: What is the metastable zone?
faq.a: It is the range of concentration and temperature in which a solution is supersaturated but new crystal nuclei hardly form spontaneously. It lies between the solubility and supersolubility curves, and growth of existing crystals mainly proceeds there.

faq.q: What changes the width of the metastable zone?
faq.a: Cooling rate, agitation intensity, impurities, the presence of seed crystals and the amount of solution all change it. Faster cooling gives a wider measured value, so values measured under the actual operating conditions are used.

faq.q: When should seed crystals be added?
faq.a: After the solution has crossed the solubility curve into the metastable zone and before spontaneous nucleation starts. Seeds added while the solution is still unsaturated dissolve, and seeds added too late coincide with spontaneous nucleation, so the crystal sizes are not uniform.

二次核発生.desc: The formation of new nuclei caused by crystals already present in the solution. It includes contact nucleation from collisions with the impeller, vessel walls or other crystals, and occurs even at the low supersaturation of the metastable zone.

MSMPR.desc: A model of a continuous crystallizer that is perfectly mixed and from which product is withdrawn continuously as suspension identical to the tank contents. If the growth rate does not depend on size, the population density decreases exponentially with size.

about.p: MSMPR stands for mixed-suspension, mixed-product-removal and describes a continuous crystallizer in which the suspension is perfectly mixed and product is withdrawn with the same composition and size distribution as the tank contents. It further assumes steady state, a crystal-free feed, a crystal growth rate G independent of size (the ΔL law), and no crystal breakage or agglomeration. This idealization allows the size distribution to be expressed by just two quantities: the nucleation rate and the growth rate. It is easiest to understand as the crystallizer counterpart of the CSTR among reactors.

Writing the number of crystals between sizes L and L + dL as n dL, the steady-state population balance is G(dn/dL) + n/τ = 0, giving n = n⁰exp(−L/(Gτ)), where τ is the mean residence time. A plot of ln n against L is a straight line with slope −1/(Gτ) and intercept n⁰, and the nucleation rate is B⁰ = n⁰G. For example, a slope of −0.020 μm⁻¹ with τ = 30 min gives Gτ = 50 μm and G of about 2.8×10⁻⁸ m/s. Deviations from a straight line point to effects such as size-dependent growth, fines dissolution or classified product removal.

The number-mean size is Gτ, the most frequent size in the mass distribution (the dominant size) is 3Gτ, and the mass-mean size is 4Gτ; the coefficient of variation of the mass distribution is about 50%, so the distribution is wide. If the residence time is lengthened at constant suspension density, the supersaturation falls and G decreases, so the size does not grow as much as the residence time. In a system whose nucleation rate is proportional to the cube of G, doubling τ increases the dominant size only about 1.26 times. When large crystals are wanted, fines dissolution or classified product removal is added.

faq.q: What does MSMPR stand for?
faq.a: It stands for mixed-suspension, mixed-product-removal: a continuous crystallizer from whose perfectly mixed suspension the product is withdrawn in the same state as the tank contents.

faq.q: What can be learned from an MSMPR size distribution?
faq.a: The slope of the straight line of ln n against size gives Gτ and the intercept gives n⁰; with the residence time, the growth rate G and the nucleation rate B⁰ = n⁰G follow.

faq.q: Why is the size distribution of MSMPR product wide?
faq.a: Because the tank is perfectly mixed, the crystal residence times follow an exponential distribution: crystals that stayed long are large, and those that left soon are withdrawn while still small. The coefficient of variation of the mass distribution is about 50%.

ΔL法則.desc: McCabe's empirical rule that geometrically similar crystals grow by the same length ΔL under the same conditions regardless of their size. Smaller seeds therefore grow more in terms of size ratio.

貧溶媒晶析.desc: Crystallization in which a solvent that dissolves the solute poorly (an antisolvent) is added to lower the solubility and create supersaturation. It needs no temperature change and suits heat-sensitive substances, but supersaturation tends to become locally high at the addition point.

結晶多形.desc: The ability of a substance of the same chemical composition to adopt different crystal structures. Each polymorph has a different solubility, melting point and dissolution rate, and at a given temperature the less soluble form is the stable one.

オストワルド熟成.desc: The phenomenon in which, because smaller particles have a slightly higher solubility, small crystals in a suspension dissolve and large crystals grow. The number of crystals decreases and the mean size increases.

種晶.desc: Small crystals added to a supersaturated solution at the start of crystallization. They provide sites for solute deposition within the metastable zone and are used to control crystal size and polymorph.

動力数.desc: The dimensionless agitation power Np = P/(ρN³D⁵). It is inversely proportional to the impeller Reynolds number in the laminar regime, and nearly constant at a value set by the impeller shape in the turbulent regime of a baffled tank.

about.p: The power number is the agitation power P made dimensionless with the liquid density ρ, rotational speed N and impeller diameter D: Np = P/(ρN³D⁵). Once the impeller and tank geometry are fixed, Np is a function only of the impeller Reynolds number Re = ρND²/μ and is summarized as an Np–Re curve. Power is found from P = NpρN³D⁵; for example, an impeller with Np = 5.0, D = 0.20 m and N = 3.0 s⁻¹ in water needs about 43 W. Because power is proportional to the cube of speed and the fifth power of impeller diameter, the choice of speed and diameter strongly affects motor size.

In the laminar regime, below Re of about 10, viscous forces dominate, Np·Re is constant, and P is proportional to μN²D³ and independent of density. In the turbulent regime, above Re of about 10⁴, Np is nearly constant in a baffled tank, and P is proportional to ρN³D⁵ and independent of viscosity. In the transitional regime between them Np changes gradually with Re, so it is read from the curve. In an unbaffled tank, swirl strengthens even in the turbulent regime and Np keeps falling, so less power goes in at the same speed.

The turbulent Np differs greatly with impeller shape: about 5 for a six-blade Rushton turbine, around 1–2 for a 45° pitched-blade turbine, and around 0.3 for an airfoil-shaped axial impeller (hydrofoil). An impeller with a large Np puts in more power at the same speed and suits shear and gas dispersion. Np is basically found by measuring the shaft torque T and using P = 2πNT; deriving it from the motor input power includes losses and gives values that are too high. Aeration forms gas cavities and lowers Np, so gassed values are treated separately.

faq.q: What is the power number?
faq.a: It is the dimensionless number Np = P/(ρN³D⁵), the agitation power divided by the liquid density, the cube of the speed and the fifth power of the impeller diameter. It shows how readily an impeller draws power and is nearly constant in the turbulent regime.

faq.q: How is agitation power found from the power number?
faq.a: Read Np at the operating conditions from the Np–Re curve and substitute it into P = NpρN³D⁵. In the turbulent regime Np can be taken as constant, so power is proportional to the cube of speed and the fifth power of impeller diameter.

faq.q: What is the power number of a Rushton turbine?
faq.a: About 5 in the turbulent regime of a baffled tank. Under the same conditions a pitched-blade turbine is around 1–2 and an airfoil axial impeller around 0.3, so it differs greatly with impeller shape.

撹拌レイノルズ数.desc: The dimensionless number Re = ρND²/μ (N the rotational speed, D the impeller diameter) that characterizes the flow in a stirred tank. Below about 10 the flow is regarded as laminar, and above about 10⁴ as turbulent.

バッフル.desc: A vertical plate mounted on the wall of a stirred tank. It suppresses swirl and vortex formation, creating axial and radial flow that improves power input and mixing. Four baffles about 1/10 to 1/12 of the tank diameter wide are standard.

ラシュトンタービン.desc: A radial-flow impeller with six flat blades mounted around a disk. Its turbulent power number is large, about 5, and its strong shear suits gas dispersion.

吐出流量数.desc: The dimensionless impeller discharge flow rate Nq = Q/(ND³). It is nearly constant in the turbulent regime and is used to estimate the circulation time V/Q and the mixing time.

混合時間.desc: The time for the concentration of a tracer added to a stirred tank to reach a specified uniformity (for example 95%) throughout the tank. In the turbulent regime its product with the rotational speed, N·θm, is nearly constant.

about.p: The mixing time θm is the time from adding a small amount of tracer to the tank until the variation in concentration in the tank falls within a chosen range. The 95% mixing time, until the concentration stays within ±5% of the final value, is commonly used. Measurement methods include adding brine and following it with a conductivity meter, the decolorization method, which watches until an indicator's color disappears on acid–base neutralization, and following a temperature change. The value depends on the position and number of detectors and on how uniformity is defined, so measurement conditions must match when values are compared.

In the turbulent regime, for the same tank and impeller, N·θm is nearly constant, so the mixing time is inversely proportional to the rotational speed. If the power number is constant in the turbulent regime, power is proportional to N³, so halving the mixing time takes 8 times the power. Taking as a guide the circulation time V/Q, in which the tank contents pass once through the impeller discharge flow Q = NqND³, the mixing time is often several times this. In the transitional and laminar regimes, N·θm grows as Re decreases, and for viscous liquids the mixing time becomes extremely long unless close-clearance impellers are used.

When a tank is scaled up with geometric similarity at constant power per unit volume, the rotational speed falls, so the mixing time increases, about 1.6 times for a doubled impeller diameter. Keeping the mixing time the same requires scaling up at unchanged speed, but then power per unit volume grows with the square of the impeller diameter, which is often impractical. For fast mixing-sensitive reactions, or processes where nonuniform temperature or pH is a problem, the longer mixing time is therefore compensated by measures such as feeding near the impeller or lowering the feed rate.

faq.q: What is mixing time?
faq.a: It is the time for the concentration of a substance added to a stirred tank to reach a chosen uniformity throughout the tank, for example within ±5% of the final concentration. It is a representative measure of how fast mixing is.

faq.q: What happens to the mixing time when the speed is raised?
faq.a: In the turbulent regime N·θm is nearly constant, so the mixing time shortens in inverse proportion to the speed. The power, however, increases with the cube of the speed.

faq.q: Why does the mixing time become longer in large tanks?
faq.a: Scaling up at constant power per unit volume lowers the rotational speed, and with N·θm constant the mixing time increases. Doubling the impeller diameter makes it about 1.6 times longer.

完全浮遊化回転数.desc: The minimum rotational speed Njs at which no particles remain on the bottom of a stirred tank. In Zwietering's correlation it increases with the density difference between particles and liquid and is inversely proportional to about the 0.85 power of the impeller diameter.

ヘリカルリボン翼.desc: A close-clearance impeller for viscous liquids that rotates a helical band near the tank wall. With a diameter of 0.9 or more of the tank diameter, it creates top-to-bottom circulation throughout the tank even in the laminar regime.
